newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian economy report sidesteps worries - papers.
newsitem.headline: Indian economy report sidesteps worries - papers.

text.p: India's annual report on the economy has underlined the government's commitment to reforms but skirted a worrying industrial slowdown and erosion of investor confidence, newspapers said on Wednesday.
"The Economic Survey...is remarkable for the vehemence with which it advertises the success of economic reforms," the Pioneer newspaper said in an editorial.
"Clearly, therefore, the document seeks to set at rest any doubts about the United Front's commitment to the reforms."

In its Economic Survey for 1996/97 (April-March), the centre-left government said a liberalisation programme launched in 1991 had placed India, with seven percent average annual growth, among the top 10 economic performers in the world.
The survey -- traditionally released by the Finance Ministry before the federal budget -- acknowledged the future is clouded by infrastructure bottlenecks, rising inflation and sluggish exports.
The government's proposed budget for the 1997/98 financial year beginning on April 1 will be released on Friday at 5 p.m. (1130 GMT).
Newspapers said the Economic Survey glossed over a slowdown in consumer demand, slack bank lending and a slump in share and real estate prices.
"The Economic Survey for 1996/97 is less remarkable for what it says than for what it leaves out," the Times of India said in an editorial headlined "Partial Picture".
"The survey acknowledges the sluggishness apparent in the industrial goods sector, rightly attributing this to infrastructure bottlenecks, particularly power," the paper said.

"However, it seems to have deliberately downplayed the demand side of the picture." Industrial growth as measured by the index of industrial production slowed to 9.8 percent during April-October 1996, from 11.7 percent a year earlier.
The Business Standard newspaper said a sharp decline in loan sanctions and a fall in domestic equity offerings indicated a "collapse in private investment".

The newspaper said the survey "notes a slight increase in the index for capital goods, and thinks this shows increased competitiveness; no wonder it concludes that the slowdown in consumer durables output means that its growth will require greater competitiveness".

The Observer newspaper said there was no assurance in the survey that the fiscal deficit, which stood at 5.8 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1995/96, would be trimmed to five percent in 1996/97 in line with the government's target.

"While the forthcoming budget should provide an insight into the government's fiscal policies, structural deficiencies in the economy are far more formidable to be tackled by budgetary dispensation alone," the Observer said.
"The survey hardly makes us wiser on removing these deficiencies -- except for restating the obvious."
